question: Statement 1: A browser cache stores static webpage elements like images and scripts locally to speed up subsequent load times. Statement 2: Cookies store active user session tokens and shopping cart configurations. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Browser cache saves rich media and structural files locally on the hard drive to reduce network bandwidth usage and latency. Step 2: Cookies are tiny key-value pairs used by web servers to track user state, preferences, and session persistence. Step 3: Both statements correctly state the unique roles of these client-side data stores.
trick: Trap: Candidates frequently mix up Cache and Cookies. Remember: Cache is all about SPEED (loading images faster). Cookies are all about MEMORY (remembering login sessions and cart items)!
tip: Cache accelerates loading speed; cookies track session state and identity profiles.

question: Match List I (URL Component) with List II (Anatomy Classification) based on the URL 'https://sub.example.in/login.php'. List I: A. https, B. sub.example.in, C. .in. List II: 1. Domain Name, 2. Top-Level Domain (TLD), 3. Protocol. Codes:
explanation: Step 1: 'https' specifies the secure transfer protocol. Step 2: 'sub.example.in' represents the full domain name string (including the subdomain 'sub'). Step 3: '.in' is the country-code Top-Level Domain (ccTLD) representing India.
trick: Trap: The TLD is only the absolute trailing block (.in), not the entire domain name string.
tip: Protocol precedes the domain; Top-Level Domain forms the very end of the domain string.

question: Statement 1: Web crawling is the phase where search engine bots download webpage text and resources. Statement 2: Search engine indexing is the logical categorization and storage of that crawled text within a master database. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Web Crawlers systematically travel from link to link downloading raw data. Step 2: Indexing parses that raw data, builds an inverted index, and saves it in data centers for instant query evaluation. Step 3: Both descriptions are technically accurate.
trick: Trap: Crawling discovers the web pages, but indexing is what actually makes them searchable on Google!
tip: Crawling is discovery via links; indexing is structured organization in a database.

question: Match List I (Data Item) with List II (Maximum Email Transmission Boundary). List I: A. Standard Gmail attachment limit, B. Total email size including overhead encodings, C. File size triggering automated Google Drive link conversion. List II: 1. Anything strictly greater than 25 MB, 2. 25 MB, 3. 25 MB. Codes:
explanation: Step 1: Gmail caps native inline file attachments at 25 MB. Step 2: The combined payload limit for an email is 25 MB. Step 3: If a user selects files totaling more than 25 MB, Gmail uploads them to Google Drive and inserts a link instead.
trick: Trap: Base64 encoding inflates attachment sizes by roughly 33%. A 20 MB binary file might fail if total email size crosses 25 MB!
tip: The magic size threshold for standard Gmail attachments is exactly 25 MB.

question: Statement 1: Clearing your browser's cookies will log you out of active shopping sessions but keep saved webpage layouts intact. Statement 2: Clearing your browser's cache will delete your stored automated passwords. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Session states are controlled by cookies; removing them forces re-authentication. Web layouts are in the cache, so Statement 1 is true. Step 2: Passwords are saved in a distinct credential manager subsystem, not in the image/file cache. Statement 2 is false.
trick: Trap: Cache has no connection to password forms. Deleting cache only forces the browser to download images again.
tip: Cookies store identity tokens; cache only stores visual files and code scripts.

question: Match List I (Search Engine Mechanism) with List II (Technical Term). List I: A. Automated link follower software, B. Data parsing file containing directory rules for bots, C. The priority ranking algorithm. List II: 1. robots.txt, 2. Spider / Bot, 3. PageRank. Codes:
explanation: Step 1: Automated link-following programs are web crawlers, often called spiders or bots. Step 2: 'robots.txt' is a text file placed at the root directory to tell bots which directories to avoid. Step 3: PageRank evaluates link structures to rank relevance.
trick: Trap: Robots.txt does not block hackers. It is a polite suggestion that good crawlers choose to obey.
tip: Spiders discover links; robots.txt restricts spiders; PageRank scores popularity.

question: Statement 1: The 'www' portion in 'https://www.gov.in' is an absolute requirement for every single website on the internet. Statement 2: The 'www' is technically a subdomain name designated by the domain administrator. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Many modern web structures use naked domains (e.g., 'https://example.com') without the 'www'. Statement 1 is false. Step 2: The 'www' (World Wide Web) string is simply a traditional subdomain choice pointing to web servers, making Statement 2 true.
trick: Trap: 'www' is not a protocol or a core internet rule. It is just a highly popular subdomain name.
tip: 'www' is a optional subdomain; modern web architecture can function perfectly without it.

question: Match List I (Cookie Classification) with List II (Lifecycle Behavior). List I: A. Session Cookie, B. Persistent Cookie, C. Third-Party Cookie. List II: 1. Retained on the hard drive for a defined period or until expiration, 2. Dropped by a domain other than the one shown in the address bar, 3. Flushed from RAM instantly when the browser tab closes. Codes:
explanation: Step 1: Session cookies track short-term states in temporary memory (RAM) and disappear upon closing the tab. Step 2: Persistent cookies store preferences on the storage drive across multiple browser sessions. Step 3: Third-party cookies are tracked by advertising networks across different websites.
trick: Trap: Third-party cookies are targeted for cross-site tracking. This is why browsers are phase-blocking them.
tip: Session = RAM based; Persistent = Hard drive based; Third-Party = Cross-site tracking.

question: Statement 1: A deep link is a URL that points specifically to a website's primary home page. Statement 2: A query string in a URL begins with a question mark symbol (?) and carries data parameters to the server. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: A deep link bypasses the home page to point directly to a specific internal piece of content. Statement 1 is false. Step 2: URL parameters use key-value format following a '?' symbol (e.g., ?search=ssc) to send data inputs, making Statement 2 true.
trick: Trap: Everything following the '?' in a URL is variable data payload being passed directly to the backend application.
tip: Query string starts with '?'. Deep links target inner specific content paths.

question: Match List I (Web Concept) with List II (Primary Technical Limitation). List I: A. Browser Cache, B. First-Party Cookie, C. Gmail Attachment. List II: 1. Max size capping of 4 KB per single file, 2. 25 MB per outbound message, 3. Hard drive storage allocation limits. Codes:
explanation: Step 1: Cache is bounded by system disk thresholds. Step 2: Standard cookies have a strict maximum size limit of 4 KB per cookie file. Step 3: Gmail stops attachments exceeding 25 MB.
trick: Trap: Cookies are text files and have a very low 4 KB capacity limit. Do not confuse them with local storage pools.
tip: Cookie cap = 4 KB; Gmail cap = 25 MB; Cache cap = Dynamic disk partition.

question: Statement 1: The 'robots.txt' file is placed in the admin dashboard subfolder of a website to hide pages. Statement 2: Search engine bots must strictly locate the robots.txt file at the root directory of a domain. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Bots check the root folder first (e.g., example.com/robots.txt). Subfolders are ignored during initialization, so Statement 1 is false. Step 2: The standard requires root directory placement for crawling permission parsing, making Statement 2 true.
trick: Trap: If robots.txt is not at the absolute root of the domain, search engine spiders will completely ignore it.
tip: Robots.txt must be at the root level of the web directory layout.

question: Match List I (Top-Level Domain Class) with List II (Target Entity). List I: A. .edu, B. .org, C. .mil. List II: 1. Military organizations, 2. Non-profit entities, 3. Educational institutions. Codes:
explanation: Step 1: .edu is reserved for schools and academic institutions. Step 2: .org traditionally designates non-commercial or non-profit organizations. Step 3: .mil is exclusively utilized by defense and military systems.
trick: Trap: While anyone can buy a .org domain today, .edu and .mil require strict background authorization credentials.
tip: .edu = Education; .org = Organization; .mil = Military network segments.

question: Statement 1: A user visiting an e-commerce site can disable cookies entirely and still stay logged into their profile across page refreshes. Statement 2: Disabling the browser cache entirely causes a website to download identical image assets every time a page shifts. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Disabling cookies destroys state memory, logging the user out on every page reload. Statement 1 is false. Step 2: Without a cache, the browser cannot load files locally, forcing a fresh download for every asset on every page view. Statement 2 is true.
trick: Trap: Turn off cookies, and web applications become 'amnesiacs'—they won't remember who you are after clicking a link.
tip: No cookies = No active session memory; No cache = Slower repeated loading times.

question: Match List I (HTTP Status Code group) with List II (Server/Client State Category). List I: A. 2xx, B. 4xx, C. 5xx. List II: 1. Server-side Error anomalies, 2. Success confirmations, 3. Client-side Request anomalies. Codes:
explanation: Step 1: 200 OK falls into the 2xx success family. Step 2: 404 Not Found indicates a client-side bad destination query (4xx). Step 3: 500 Internal Server Error represents systemic host-side failure (5xx).
trick: Trap: 404 means YOU requested a bad page link. 500 means the SERVER crashed running code.
tip: 2xx = OK; 4xx = Client mistake (404); 5xx = Server crash (500).

question: Statement 1: In the URL framework, 'http://' and 'https://' behave identically regarding transit data privacy. Statement 2: The 's' in HTTPS indicates data payload wrapping with SSL or TLS cryptography. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: HTTP sends data in clear plain text, whereas HTTPS encrypts the stream. Statement 1 is false. Step 2: The 's' explicitly stands for Secure, implementing SSL/TLS network layers, making Statement 2 true.
trick: Trap: Never type passwords on standard HTTP input boxes; sniffing tools can capture them easily.
tip: HTTPS encrypts data streams; basic HTTP exposes data in clear text.

question: Match List I (Search Engine Component) with List II (Core Functional Purpose). List I: A. User Query Interface, B. Inverted Index Database, C. Crawler Policy. List II: 1. Decides the frequency and order of scanning target links, 2. Evaluates consumer input text strings against indexed terms, 3. A structured lookup catalog linking words to their containing webpage IDs. Codes:
explanation: Step 1: The user interface matches typed keywords against index entries. Step 2: An inverted index is a database mapping words to web page locations. Step 3: Crawler policy sets boundaries and priority schedules for discovery bots.
trick: Trap: Search engines do not search the live web when you type a query; they search their internal stored index database!
tip: Google queries its pre-compiled internal database, not the active live web.

question: Statement 1: A cookie can execute binary system applications on a user's computer hard drive to clean up disk space. Statement 2: Cookies are passive text strings that cannot run code natively. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Cookies are flat text datasets, completely incapable of execution or compiling commands. Statement 1 is false. Step 2: Because they are non-executable text records, they pose no direct virus propagation capabilities, making Statement 2 true.
trick: Trap: Cookies are data records, not code programs. They can track you, but they can't infect your files.
tip: Cookies are flat text structures; they cannot execute or delete system software.

question: Match List I (URL Specific Component) with List II (Functional Segment Designation) based on the URL 'https://example.com:8080/store/items.html'. List I: A. :8080, B. /store/items.html, C. example.com. List II: 1. Network Port Number, 2. Server Resource File Path, 3. Host / Domain Name. Codes:
explanation: Step 1: The numeric value trailing the colon indicates the network port assignment. Step 2: The path string dictates the logical subdirectory folder mapping on the host storage. Step 3: 'example.com' provides the host network identity locator.
trick: Trap: If no port is specified in a URL, the browser assumes default 80 for HTTP or 443 for HTTPS.
tip: Colon trailing a domain maps a non-standard network port location manually.

question: Statement 1: Sending an email attachment size of 30 MB can be done natively via Gmail without using any cloud storage systems. Statement 2: Gmail uses a mandatory 25 MB limit for standard data attachment pathways. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: A 30 MB file triggers automatic offloading to Google Drive cloud storage. Native attachment fails, so Statement 1 is false. Step 2: The standard outbound attachment cap is exactly 25 MB, making Statement 2 true.
trick: Trap: Large files are shared as hyperlinks, not as raw data attachments in the message body.
tip: Files over 25 MB turn into cloud share links inside Gmail.

question: Match List I (Web Concept) with List II (Geographical Context or Identifier). List I: A. Country-Code Top-Level Domain (ccTLD), B. Generic Top-Level Domain (gTLD), C. Subdomain block. List II: 1. .com, 2. .in, 3. www. Codes:
explanation: Step 1: '.in' indicates a country specific country-code Top-Level Domain for India. Step 2: '.com' represents a non-geographical commercial generic Top-Level Domain. Step 3: 'www' acts as a local subdomain layer.
trick: Trap: ccTLD formats always utilize a two-letter structural design (.in, .uk, .ca).
tip: ccTLDs use two characters to target localized geographic regions.

question: Statement 1: 'Incognito' or private browsing modes entirely block your Internet Service Provider from tracking which domains you visit. Statement 2: Incognito modes merely prevent the local browser application from logging cookies, search history, and cache assets after the session ends. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Incognito blocks local tracking, but upstream servers and ISPs see the IP addresses routed, making Statement 1 false. Step 2: Private browsing is a local cleanup mechanism for cookies and historical text, making Statement 2 true.
trick: Trap: Incognito protects your privacy from people who use your computer, not from network trackers or your ISP!
tip: Incognito mode hides data locally from your device; network data remains visible.

question: Match List I (Browser State Component) with List II (Primary Mechanical Location). List I: A. Web Storage API / Cookies, B. Cached Image Assets, C. URL Autocomplete History. List II: 1. System storage drive partition, 2. Temporary internet files directory, 3. Internal text data files. Codes:
explanation: Step 1: Cookies use small text databases managed by browser configuration paths. Step 2: Cache files are located in dedicated directories on the local storage drive. Step 3: Autocomplete links utilize historical text records saved sequentially.
trick: Trap: All three items exist on your storage drive, but they are stored in distinct directories and files.
tip: Cache preserves asset files; cookies are key-value text lines.

question: Statement 1: A search engine bot follows 'nofollow' hyperlinked attributes as a priority pipeline to index new target content quickly. Statement 2: The 'nofollow' HTML attribute value instructs crawlers not to pass algorithmic endorsement score to that link destination. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Spiders bypass or ignore 'nofollow' designated pathways for structural indexing discovery. Statement 1 is false. Step 2: The primary intent of 'nofollow' is preventing search relevance manipulation via comment spam links, making Statement 2 true.
trick: Trap: Nofollow tells search engines to ignore a link's authority value during scoring evaluations.
tip: 'nofollow' tells crawlers not to associate search rank value with a link.

question: Match List I (URL Parameter Component) with List II (Syntax Indicator Rule). List I: A. Beginning of the variable sequence string, B. Separator character between discrete key-value pairs, C. Allocation character mapping a variable to a data value. List II: 1. Question Mark (?), 2. Ampersand (&), 3. Equals Sign (=). Codes:
explanation: Step 1: '?' initializes parameter data string inputs. Step 2: '&' strings separate sequential values together. Step 3: '=' links the variable name to its current data state assignment.
trick: Trap: In 'id=5&page=2', the ampersand joins the two distinct parameters together.
tip: ? starts parameters; = assigns data values; & chains parameters.

question: Statement 1: The maximum lifetime of a standard browser session cookie extends infinitely across multiple computer restarts. Statement 2: Session cookies are fundamentally stored in volatile random-access memory (RAM) and evaporate upon software closure. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Session cookies do not write to permanent storage drives, so they do not persist after closing the app. Statement 1 is false. Step 2: They are isolated to volatile memory arrays, disappearing when the process terminates, making Statement 2 true.
trick: Trap: If you close a tab and stay logged in, that is a persistent cookie, not a session cookie.
tip: Session cookies vanish when the browser process ends; persistent cookies survive restarts.

question: Match List I (Web Asset Type) with List II (Cache Benefit Rating). List I: A. Company Logo image file (.png), B. Dynamic stock market price text block, C. Framework script file (.js). List II: 1. Highly eligible for long term caching, 2. Completely ineligible for caching, 3. Highly eligible for long term caching. Codes:
explanation: Step 1: Static imagery like a logo remains fixed, making it perfect for caching. Step 2: Financial tickers change instantly; caching them displays outdated, invalid data. Step 3: Script frameworks are static core files that benefit significantly from local retention.
trick: Trap: Real-time dynamic text should never be cached, or users will see stale information.
tip: Static structural files belong in the cache; real-time variables do not.

question: Statement 1: A web crawler tracks external links but cannot explore internal architectural navigation elements. Statement 2: A crawler recursively aggregates discovered hyperlinks to expand its boundary map of available web locations. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Crawlers treat internal and external hyperlinks identically, scanning internal navigation hierarchies thoroughly. Statement 1 is false. Step 2: Recursive discovery forms the foundation of automated index scanning systems, making Statement 2 true.
trick: Trap: Spiders crawl every anchor link they discover unless explicitly blocked by directory rules.
tip: Crawlers discover pages by systematically parsing all available links on a page.

question: Match List I (E-commerce Browser Operation) with List II (Core Underlying Feature). List I: A. Keeping items safely in a shopping cart without checking out, B. Drastically reduced bandwidth usage when revisiting product categories, C. Auto-filling delivery coordinates. List II: 1. Browser Cache storage arrays, 2. Persistent Cookie tracking tokens, 3. Autofill history database parameters. Codes:
explanation: Step 1: Cart persistence across daily intervals utilizes persistent text cookies. Step 2: Asset reuse for asset loading speed maps to cache operations. Step 3: Text input storage relies on autocomplete history files.
trick: Trap: Cache speeds up layout graphics; cookies protect personalization configurations and cart choices.
tip: Cart preservation relies on cookies; faster graphic loads rely on the cache.

question: Statement 1: The string 'http://localhost' points to an active external routing infrastructure managed by an ISP. Statement 2: 'localhost' is a loopback network address pointing directly back to the user's local machine environment. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Localhost does not communicate past the network interface card out to an external network. Statement 1 is false. Step 2: It loops data directly back into the local operating software environment, making Statement 2 true.
trick: Trap: Localhost resolves internally to the IP address 127.0.0.1 without querying external DNS servers.
tip: Localhost maps internally to 127.0.0.1 for self-testing applications.

question: Match List I (Search Engine Index Failure Scenario) with List II (Probable Source Cause). List I: A. A public page completely missing from search results, B. A page showing old, outdated text from months ago, C. An error loading search interface tools. List II: 1. Search index database has not re-crawled the link yet, 2. Application connection drop, 3. Directory link blocked via 'disallow' syntax in robots.txt. Codes:
explanation: Step 1: A missing public page is often caused by a 'Disallow' rule in robots.txt blocking crawls. Step 2: Stale snippets happen when a page has changed but the crawler has not updated its index. Step 3: Interface load failures are standard application connection bugs.
trick: Trap: Search engine visibility depends entirely on allowing crawling entry via robots.txt policies.
tip: Disallow rules in robots.txt prevent automated search indexing.

question: Statement 1: Malicious programs can use third-party cookies to read files stored in your computer's Documents folder. Statement 2: Cookies are sandboxed text tracking segments constrained tightly by browser application safety frameworks. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Cookies cannot cross security parameters to read system storage files. Statement 1 is false. Step 2: Browsers strictly sandbox cookies, preventing them from accessing file arrays outside the application boundary, making Statement 2 true.
trick: Trap: Cookies can track what you browse, but they can never view your personal drive files.
tip: Cookies are sandboxed; they cannot access system hard drive directories.

question: Match List I (URL Scheme) with List II (Target Application Environment). List I: A. ftp://, B. mailto:, C. file://. List II: 1. Launches default local email transmission software client, 2. Targets file storage servers, 3. Maps local system computer storage pathways natively inside the browser. Codes:
explanation: Step 1: 'ftp://' establishes connection rules for moving files across remote servers. Step 2: 'mailto:' initializes user communication parameters inside mail software. Step 3: 'file://' instructs the browser to open files directly from the local hard drive.
trick: Trap: Not all URLs target the internet; 'file://' opens local storage assets inside the browser window.
tip: 'mailto:' triggers local mail clients; 'file://' views local computer files.

question: Statement 1: Hard reloading a page (Ctrl + F5) instructs the browser to bypass local cache storage and download everything fresh. Statement 2: Normal reloads prioritize using existing local cache data to preserve web transit bandwidth. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Ctrl + F5 clears the cache context for that specific web request, forcing a new download. Step 2: Normal execution uses locally stored assets to maximize speed and minimize bandwidth usage. Step 3: Both statements are true.
trick: Trap: If a website layout looks broken after an update, a hard refresh fixes it by updating the cache.
tip: Ctrl+F5 forces a fresh download, bypassing old local cache data.

question: Match List I (Web Domain Example) with List II (Domain Hierarchical Layer Name). List I: A. .org in 'wikipedia.org', B. 'en' in 'en.wikipedia.org', C. 'wikipedia' in 'wikipedia.org'. List II: 1. Subdomain layer, 2. Second-Level Domain (SLD), 3. Top-Level Domain (TLD). Codes:
explanation: Step 1: '.org' represents the structural Top-Level Domain block. Step 2: 'en' acts as an isolated sub-segment (subdomain) configuration. Step 3: 'wikipedia' represents the unique Second-Level Domain name registered by the organization.
trick: Trap: In domain reading, go right-to-left: TLD (.org) first, then Second-Level Domain (wikipedia).
tip: Read domain structures from right to left to understand their hierarchy.

question: Statement 1: Search engine optimization (SEO) techniques modify server scripts to alter crawler visibility patterns. Statement 2: Search engines penalize sites that show different text to discovery bots than to human visitors. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: SEO uses configuration strategies to help bots index pages accurately. Step 2: This deceptive practice is called 'cloaking', and search engines penalize it to prevent search result manipulation. Step 3: Both statements are correct.
trick: Trap: Deruptive indexing practices like cloaking can get a domain permanently banned from Google's index database.
tip: Cloaking means tricking bots with fake text, which results in blacklisting penalties.

question: Match List I (Browser Configuration Mode) with List II (Primary Technical Consequence). List I: A. Disabling Cookies entirely, B. Restricting Third-Party Cookies alone, C. Blocking all Cache storage. List II: 1. Cross-site advertisement profiling is blocked while keeping login storage working, 2. Web pages load noticeably slower on return visits, 3. User authentication profiles fail to register. Codes:
explanation: Step 1: No cookies means no persistent user sessions. Step 2: Third-party blocks stop cross-site tracking ad trackers but keep main sites working. Step 3: No cache forces full downloads on every page load, slowing performance.
trick: Trap: Blocking third-party cookies preserves privacy without breaking your main website login states.
tip: Blocking third-party cookies limits tracking networks while preserving primary website logins.

question: Statement 1: A URL must never contain spaces or specialty characters without converting them into a percent-encoded string format. Statement 2: A space character in a URL string is percent-encoded into the characters '%20'. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: URLs utilize the restricted ASCII character set; special symbols and spaces require replacement tracking structures. Step 2: The universal representation mapping a blank space element inside browser engines uses '%20' syntax. Step 3: Both statements are true.
trick: Trap: Web browsers auto-hide percent encoding visually, but the raw network link must use '%20' for spaces.
tip: URLs cannot contain raw spaces; they must use '%20' percent-encoding.

question: Match List I (Internet File System) with List II (Primary Functionality). List I: A. Sitemap (.xml), B. robots.txt, C. HTTP response headers. List II: 1. A road map file explicitly listing all active URLs to help bots index everything, 2. Text configuration controlling spider access rules, 3. Command properties telling the browser how long to cache a file. Codes:
explanation: Step 1: Sitemaps list all system URLs to help search engines discover deep pages. Step 2: Robots.txt controls directory entry rules for spiders. Step 3: Cache-Control parameters in HTTP headers tell the browser how long to cache files locally.
trick: Trap: Sitemaps guide bots to valid pages; robots.txt blocks bots from private directories.
tip: Sitemaps invite crawlers in; robots.txt sets boundaries to keep them out.

question: Statement 1: If a user sends five separate 10 MB files at once in a single Gmail message, the system will successfully send them as standard inline attachments. Statement 2: The sum of all attached files in an email must fit within the total 25 MB message payload size limit. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Five 10 MB files total 50 MB, which exceeds the 25 MB limit and triggers Google Drive conversion. Statement 1 is false. Step 2: The 25 MB attachment cap applies to the total combined size of the files, not each individual file. Statement 2 is true.
trick: Trap: The 25 MB limit applies to the sum total of all files attached to a single email, not per file!
tip: Email attachment boundaries track the cumulative sum size of all attached files.

question: Match List I (Network Path Element) with List II (Syntax Placement Separation). List I: A. Protocol marker, B. Port assignment marker, C. Anchor/Fragment identifier. List II: 1. Hash symbol (#), 2. Double slash following a colon (://), 3. Leading colon following a domain name string (:). Codes:
explanation: Step 1: Schemes/protocols use '://' to separate the protocol from the domain. Step 2: Port assignments append via a colon (:) immediately after the domain name. Step 3: Sub-page fragments use a '#' symbol to scroll directly to a specific section.
trick: Trap: Everything after the '#' symbol is processed locally by the browser and is never sent to the web server!
tip: '#' marks a page fragment location and is handled entirely by the browser.

question: Statement 1: Browser cache stores data across user profile switches, allowing user A to see cached layouts generated by user B. Statement 2: Browser cache data partitions are completely isolated per individual system user profile framework. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Operating systems isolate application directories across accounts, preventing crossover data leaks. Statement 1 is false. Step 2: Each profile manages its own separate secure cache folders, making Statement 2 true.
trick: Trap: Profile isolation ensures total confidentiality across different browser users on the same computer.
tip: Operating systems strictly separate cache and cookie histories across individual user accounts.

question: Match List I (Search Engine Index State) with List II (Operational Result). List I: A. Sandbox status, B. De-indexed status, C. Crawled but not indexed status. List II: 1. Domain explicitly deleted from the database due to violations, 2. Page found by bots but skipped due to poor quality or duplicate content, 3. Restricted visibility applied to brand new web properties. Codes:
explanation: Step 1: Search sandboxes limit visibility for new domains until they build trust. Step 2: De-indexing removes a site completely for violating quality guidelines. Step 3: Crawled but unindexed means bots scanned the page but skipped it because it was duplicate or low quality.
trick: Trap: Discovering a page does not guarantee it gets indexed. Quality checks can keep pages out of search results.
tip: Crawling only means discovery; indexing requires passing automated quality checks.

question: Statement 1: Cookies can track cross-site browsing history only if third-party cookies are allowed by the browser. Statement 2: First-party cookies are generated by the specific domain listed in the address bar to maintain primary session state. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Advertising networks use third-party tracking cookies across partner sites to build interest profiles. Step 2: First-party cookies are created directly by the site you are visiting to remember your login and preferences. Step 3: Both statements are true.
trick: Trap: First-party cookies are safe and necessary for logins. Third-party cookies are the ones used for tracking and ads.
tip: First-party cookies keep you logged in; third-party cookies track you across different websites.

question: Match List I (URL Domain Suffix) with List II (Organizational Scope Category). List I: A. .gov, B. .net, C. .biz. List II: 1. Business and commercial entities, 2. Network infrastructure providers, 3. Government departments. Codes:
explanation: Step 1: '.gov' is restricted exclusively to official government entities. Step 2: '.net' originally targeted network technologies and ISPs. Step 3: '.biz' is a generic TLD used by commercial businesses.
trick: Trap: Like .edu, .gov domains have strict validation requirements and cannot be bought by the public.
tip: .gov indicates verified, official government network platforms.

question: Statement 1: Stored browser cache can accidentally display old information if a website updates its design but the local files haven't expired yet. Statement 2: Clearing your cache forces the browser to download the latest updates from the web server. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: If the browser loads stale files from the local cache instead of requesting updates, the layout can look broken. Step 2: Clearing the cache deletes these local files, forcing a fresh download of the new site design. Step 3: Both statements are true.
trick: Trap: Web developers alter file names (like style.v2.css) to force browsers to clear out old cache versions automatically.
tip: Stale cache issues are quickly resolved by clearing temporary browser files.

question: Match List I (Web Bot Identification) with List II (Operating Identity Entity Name). List I: A. Google Search Bot, B. Bing Search Bot, C. Interface definition framework tracking bot rules. List II: 1. Bingbot, 2. Googlebot, 3. User-Agent string properties. Codes:
explanation: Step 1: Google's primary web crawler identifies itself as 'Googlebot'. Step 2: Microsoft's discovery bot uses the 'Bingbot' identifier. Step 3: The 'User-Agent' string in HTTP requests tells websites which bot or browser is visiting.
trick: Trap: Sneaky bots can fake their User-Agent string to bypass robots.txt rules. True verification requires a reverse DNS lookup.
tip: Bots use User-Agent headers to identify themselves to web servers.

question: Statement 1: Cookies can store encrypted payload text strings but cannot hold raw binary audio or video file attachments directly. Statement 2: The small 4 KB size limit makes cookies unsuitable for storing rich media files. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Cookies are simple text files meant for small strings, not complex binary attachments. Step 2: The strict 4 KB limit makes it physically impossible to store media files like images or audio inside a cookie. Step 3: Both statements are correct.
trick: Trap: Large data should be saved in IndexedDB or LocalStorage, which offer megabytes of space compared to a cookie's 4 KB.
tip: Cookies are tiny text containers limited to 4 KB of data.

question: Match List I (URL Parameter Formatting) with List II (Technical Description). List I: A. %2F, B. +, C. %3D. List II: 1. Percent-encoded representation of an equals sign (=), 2. Percent-encoded representation of a forward slash (/), 3. Alternate standard encoding for a blank space character. Codes:
explanation: Step 1: '%2F' is the encoded format for a forward slash, preventing conflicts with URL path separators. Step 2: The '+' symbol is often used as a shorthand encoding for a space inside query strings. Step 3: '%3D' represents the encoded equals sign.
trick: Trap: Slashes and equals signs are encoded in query values so the browser doesn't confuse them with structural URL layout markers.
tip: Percent-encoding replaces reserved characters with hex values to keep URLs valid.

question: Statement 1: A 'Session Fixation' attack involves manipulating browser cache assets to display fake layouts. Statement 2: Session fixation attacks exploit vulnerabilities in session cookie tracking tokens to hijack user accounts. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Session fixation is a cookie hijacking exploit, completely unrelated to browser cache mechanics. Statement 1 is false. Step 2: This attack tricks a user into using a known session ID cookie, allowing the attacker to steal the session once the user logs in. Statement 2 is true.
trick: Trap: If an attacker steals your session cookie token, they can log into your account without needing your password!
tip: Session fixation exploits session cookies to steal active logins.

question: Match List I (E-mail Size Overhead) with List II (Consequence / Technical Detail). List I: A. Base64 encoding inflation factor, B. Gmail native attachment limit boundary, C. trick: Trap: Because text encoding inflates file sizes, a 21 MB file might get blocked if the total message crosses 25 MB!
tip: Base64 text conversion increases binary file attachment sizes by about 33%.

question: Match List I with List II regarding URL structure: List I: (A) https:// (B) www.ssc.gov.in (C) .in. List II: (1) Domain Name (2) Country-code Top-Level Domain (ccTLD) (3) Protocol Scheme. Select the correct code:

question: Consider the following statements regarding local browser data: Statement 1: Browser Cache stores multimedia elements like images and scripts locally to reduce webpage load time on subsequent visits. Statement 2: Cookies are tiny text files used exclusively by the user's operating system to clear corrupted RAM blocks. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Browser Cache downloads static assets locally to boost website rendering speeds. Step 2: Cookies do not interact with OS RAM blocks; they track user authentication states and site configurations. Therefore, Statement 2 is entirely false.
trick: Trap: Candidates frequently mix up Cache and Cookies. Remember: 'Cache' is all about SPEED (loading images faster). 'Cookies' are all about MEMORY (remembering your passwords and cart items)!
tip: Cache accelerates rendering speeds. Cookies track human sessions and preferences.

question: Match List I with List II regarding Search Engine operations: List I: (A) Web Crawler (B) Indexing (C) Parsing. List II: (1) Analyzing the text and HTML tags of crawled pages to store them in a massive organized database (2) Automated scripts systematically navigating hyperlinks to discover new webpages (3) Extracting structural data fragments from a raw webpage document. Select the correct code:
explanation: Step 1: A Web Crawler (or spider/bot) systematically wanders across web links to fetch pages. Step 2: Indexing systematically categorizes and saves those crawled pages into the search engine's database directory. Step 3: Parsing converts raw markup into clean code parameters.
trick: Trap: Believing search engines search the live web instantly when you click 'Search'. They query their pre-built 'Index' database, which was compiled days before by Crawlers!
tip: Crawlers discover pages. Indexing logs data. Search engines read the index.

question: Consider the following statements regarding email communication bounds: Statement 1: The standard maximum payload size for a single inbound or outbound attachment in Gmail is strictly limited to 25 MB. Statement 2: If an attachment exceeds 25 MB, Gmail converts the entire communication layer into an encrypted FTP pipe automatically. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Standard SMTP infrastructure limits file uploads, and Gmail caps single attachment files at 25 MB. Step 2: If a file exceeds this size, Gmail prompts the user to upload the file to Google Drive instead of converting to an encrypted FTP pipe.
trick: Trap: Thinking email can handle massive files directly. The underlying MIME protocol encoding inflates files by 33%, forcing strict size caps like 25 MB.
tip: Gmail enforces a strict 25 MB threshold for basic document attachments.

question: Match List I with List II regarding Top-Level Domain classifications: List I: (A) .org (B) .edu (C) .mil. List II: (1) Restricted to accredited educational institutions (2) Reserved exclusively for military frameworks (3) Originally designated for non-profit organizations. Select the correct code:
explanation: Step 1: '.org' stands for organization, historically non-profit. Step 2: '.edu' stands for education, strictly limited to schools and colleges. Step 3: '.mil' stands for military, reserved for defense networks.
trick: Trap: Anyone can purchase a '.org' domain today without proof of non-profit status. However, '.edu' and '.mil' require valid legal credentials.
tip: TLDs categorize websites by domain function, access rules, or geography.

question: Consider the following statements regarding the Robots.txt file: Statement 1: Robots.txt is a plain text configuration file placed in a website's root directory to instruct web crawlers which parts of the site they are permitted to scan. Statement 2: Robots.txt acts as an unbreachable encryption firewall that physically blocks hackers from accessing sensitive backend databases. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Robots.txt governs crawler behavior through directive parameters. Step 2: It is a public file and completely relies on the honor system; it cannot block malicious actors or act as an encryption firewall.
trick: Trap: Putting secret file paths inside robots.txt to hide them. Malicious hackers read public robots.txt files first to find vulnerable paths!
tip: Robots.txt suggests crawler boundaries; it provides absolutely zero security.

question: Match List I with List II regarding URL query parameters: List I: (A) Query string delimiter (B) Parameter separator (C) Anchor / Fragment identifier. List II: (1) & (2) # (3) ?. Select the correct code:
explanation: Step 1: The '?' symbol acts as the delimiter separating the base URL from custom query strings. Step 2: The '&' symbol separates individual key-value pairs within a query. Step 3: The '#' symbol jumps directly to a specific HTML element ID on a page.
trick: Trap: Confusing the query string with an anchor. Browsers never pass the '#' fragment symbol or its following text to the web server; it remains strictly internal to scroll your local screen!
tip: ? starts queries, & stacks parameters, # jumps down pages.

question: Consider the following statements regarding browser session cookies: Statement 1: Transient (Session) cookies are stored temporarily in volatile memory and are completely wiped when the user closes the web browser window. Statement 2: Persistent tracking cookies are permanently hardcoded directly into the computer's physical motherboard BIOS chip. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Session cookies track short interactions like shopping cart items and expire when the browser shuts down. Step 2: Persistent cookies are saved as standard flat text files on the local hard drive, never inside the motherboard BIOS chip.
trick: Trap: Believing tracking software can modify hardware silicon layers. Cookies are purely high-level browser profile configuration files.
tip: Transient cookies die with the browser; persistent cookies live on disk.

question: Match List I with List II regarding web resource pathing concepts: List I: (A) Absolute URL (B) Relative URL (C) Base URL. List II: (1) Points to a file relative to the current folder location without specifying a protocol scheme (2) The foundational directory path from which all internal links extend (3) Contains the complete internet coordinates including scheme, host, and full directory path. Select the correct code:
explanation: Step 1: Absolute URLs provide unambiguous global coordinate definitions. Step 2: Relative links rely entirely on the browser's current active folder tracking. Step 3: Base URLs provide the anchor path to rebuild relative strings.
trick: Trap: Using Relative links inside an email newsletter template. If a subscriber clicks an internal relative link from an email app, it will break completely because there is no base website folder context!
tip: Absolute links contain the complete domain address. Relative paths append local directories.

question: Consider the following statements regarding browser data clearing: Statement 1: Clearing browser cache forces the application to re-download the newest media content directly from the host web server upon the next visit. Statement 2: Clearing cookies will automatically remove all downloaded JPEG graphics from your local hard drive cache directory. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Flushing cache flushes out stale layout templates, enforcing fresh assets downloads. Step 2: Cookies hold session data strings, not graphics. Clearing cookies logs you out of profiles but leaves image cache untouched.
trick: Trap: Wondering why a webpage design layout fix isn't displaying on your screen. The browser is lazy and reading old data from its hidden cache! Clear your cache to force a design update.
tip: Flushing cache updates visuals. Flushing cookies signs you out of websites.

question: Match List I with List II regarding top search engine crawlers: List I: (A) Googlebot (B) Bingbot (C) Slurp. List II: (1) Yahoo's proprietary indexing crawler script (2) Microsoft's enterprise web scanning agent (3) Google's core discovery crawler infrastructure. Select the correct code:
explanation: Step 1: Googlebot scans and maps internet indices for Google. Step 2: Bingbot tracks nodes for Microsoft Bing. Step 3: Slurp is the historical designation for Yahoo's indexing engine crawler system.
trick: Trap: Assuming all traffic is human. Up to 40% of standard website bandwidth is consumed by automated crawlers updating corporate indices!
tip: Googlebot, Bingbot, and Slurp are automated indexing web robots.

question: Consider the following statements regarding URL Encoding: Statement 1: URLs can only be transmitted over the internet using the standard ASCII character set. Statement 2: Spaces within a URL are mathematically invalid and are automatically encoded into '%20' or '+' characters. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: RFC guidelines restrict URL formats strictly to unreserved ASCII strings. Step 2: Non-ASCII characters or spaces are converted to percentage-encoded hex numbers, translating a space character directly to '%20'.
trick: Trap: Trying to type a clean sentence in a link string. The browser will convert it to an unreadable wall of percent signs and hex numbers to ensure it complies with ASCII requirements!
tip: URL Encoding translates non-ASCII inputs into valid hexadecimal percentage formats safely.

question: Match List I with List II regarding browser cookie attributes: List I: (A) HttpOnly (B) Secure (C) SameSite. List II: (1) Restricts the cookie from being sent with cross-site requests, mitigating CSRF attacks (2) Blocks client-side scripts like JavaScript from reading the cookie data, preventing XSS thefts (3) Dictates that the cookie can only be transmitted over encrypted HTTPS tunnels. Select the correct code:
explanation: Step 1: 'HttpOnly' isolates cookie data blocks from cross-site scripting injections. Step 2: The 'Secure' flag drops traffic transmission if an unsecured HTTP link is used. Step 3: 'SameSite' limits structural visibility during context switches.
trick: Trap: Thinking HTTPS automatically locks everything. Without the 'HttpOnly' flag, a hacker using a dirty script line can steal your active session token directly from the browser context!
tip: HttpOnly blocks script access. Secure blocks unencrypted network transport.

question: Consider the following statements regarding Search Engine optimization index tracking: Statement 1: Deep Web content refers to pages that are hidden behind user paywalls, login boxes, or explicit unindexed parameters, rendering them invisible to standard Crawlers. Statement 2: The Dark Web consists of standard public HTML documents that are easily listed by Googlebot search queries. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Deep web encompasses standard data files like banking portals or private inboxes that scripts cannot crawl. Step 2: The Dark web requires specialized overlay browsers like Tor to access. It completely blocks standard tracking engines, so Statement 2 is completely false.
trick: Trap: Confusing Deep Web with Dark Web. Your personal private Gmail inbox is 'Deep Web' because Googlebot cannot list it without your login!
tip: Deep web is unindexed utility data. Dark web requires specific encrypted routers.

question: Match List I with List II regarding special alphanumeric structures: List I: (A) IP Address (B) Port Number (C) URL. List II: (1) 192.168.1.1 (2) https://www.bank.com/index.html (3) 443. Select the correct code:

tip: IP spots nodes. Ports handle application doors. URLs locate individual web resources.

question: Consider the following statements regarding First-Party vs Third-Party cookies: Statement 1: First-Party cookies are generated directly by the host domain you are actively visiting to preserve your active login session state. Statement 2: Third-Party cookies are injected by cross-site ad tracking networks to map your browsing history across entirely different web domains. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: First-party cookies maintain user convenience metrics locally. Step 2: Third-party cookies track user tracking maps invisibly for ad distribution networks. Both statements are technically and functionally correct.

tip: First-party tracks you on-site. Third-party follows you across the net.

question: Match List I with List II regarding specialized URL anatomy fields: List I: (A) Subdomain (B) Top-Level Domain (C) Path directory. List II: (1) /exams/tier2/ (2) blog.website.com (3) .gov. Select the correct code:

question: Consider the following statements regarding search engine Index structure: Statement 1: Search engine optimization indexing maps strings utilizing an Inverted Index, matching singular text keywords directly to all verified URLs that contain them. question: Match List I with List II regarding data constraints and network limits: List I: (A) Gmail attachment threshold (B) Maximum standard URL string visibility length (3) Cookie payload tracking size. question: Consider the following statements regarding the dynamic interaction of cache memory: Statement 1: Browsers use a HTTP header called 'Cache-Control' to determine how long a local file asset can be safely stored before checking the server for updates. tip: Cache rules are dictated by server headers, but can lock in obsolete graphics.

question: Match List I with List II regarding browser cookie behavior flags: List I: (A) Session Cookie (B) Persistent Cookie (C) Zombie Cookie. List II: (1) Automatically recreates itself using hidden local storage backups after a user deletes it (2) Disappears from memory instantly when the active browser tab context terminates (3) Utilizes an explicit 'Expires' or 'Max-Age' attribute stamp to survive computer reboots. question: Consider the following statements regarding Search Engine ranking parameters: Statement 1: Crawlers evaluate internal link tracking structures, checking page layout hierarchies and depth to judge domain link values. tip: Crawlers trace architectural links closely, tracking stability metrics for rank indexing.

question: Match List I with List II regarding protocol and data mappings: List I: (A) URL scheme identifier (B) Web database queries (C) Static media tracking. List II: (1) Browser Cache (2) HTTP / HTTPS (3) Query Strings. Select the correct code:

question: Consider the following statements regarding URL domain architecture: Statement 1: In the URL 'https://sub.example.com/index.html', the string 'example' is classified as a Top-Level Domain. tip: .com is the TLD. DNS matches alphabetic domain labels to physical numeric IP destinations.

question: Match List I with List II regarding user preference management tools: List I: (A) Shopping Cart persistence (B) Static layout background image acceleration (C) Deep link index tracking discovery. List II: (1) Web Crawler (2) Persistent Cookie (3) Browser Cache. Select the correct code:
explanation: Step 1: Persistent cookies track user shopping arrays during disconnect cycles. Step 2: Cache parameters prevent downloading heavy layout graphics on every view change step. Step 3: Crawlers scour structural link configurations to build indexing directories.

tip: Cookies log states, cache holds heavy local files, crawlers map database indices.

question: Consider the following statements regarding the 'Incognito / Private' browsing mode: Statement 1: Incognito mode stops your Internet Service Provider (ISP) and government defense frameworks from tracking your data traffic maps across the web. Statement 2: Incognito mode simply prevents the local computer application from saving history records, temporary cache items, and cookies during the session. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Incognito mode provides zero external network path masking; routers track your traffic completely. Statement 1 is false. Step 2: It is strictly a local privacy wrapper that deletes cookies and history files when you exit the app window. Statement 2 is correct.
trick: Trap: Believing Incognito makes you invisible. It only hides your browsing tracks from family members sharing your computer, not from your boss or your ISP network routers!
tip: Incognito mode limits local device database logs; it provides absolute zero network privacy protection.

question: Match List I with List II regarding technical URL structure symbols: List I: (A) Username/Password indicator delimiter (B) Port tracking delimiter (C) Directory routing indicator. List II: (1) : (2) / (3) @. Select the correct code:
explanation: Step 1: Legacy inline authentication layouts use '@' strings (e.g., user:pass@domain.com). Step 2: Port allocations attach via colons ':' (e.g., host:8080). Step 3: Slashes '/' map filesystem tree directory configurations.

tip: Colons mark custom ports. Slashes route file structural systems. At signs delineate raw logins.

question: Consider the following statements regarding Search Engine optimization crawling hurdles: Statement 1: Broken redirects (loops) trap web crawlers in infinite cycles, forcing them to exhaust their assigned processing resource limits (Crawl Budget). Statement 2: Crawlers can parse text characters embedded directly inside hardcoded flash memory objects or complex video tracks natively without processing scripts. explanation: Step 1: Interlocking redirect actions trap spiders, burning their temporary site connection limits (Crawl budget). Step 2: Spiders are fundamentally text processors; they cannot natively watch video files to pull text values out of media tracks without metadata descriptions. Statement 2 is false.
trick: Trap: Creating broken redirect loops on a site. Crawlers will get stuck, panic, and completely stop listing your healthy pages to protect their server limits!
tip: Redirect loops drain bot crawl budgets. Spiders prioritize parsing text metadata over reading multimedia binaries.

question: Match List I with List II regarding browser cookie limit behaviors: List I: (A) Max cookie size footprint (B) Maximum standard cookie count restriction per unique host domain (C) Cookie lifespan if zero attributes are defined. List II: (1) 20 to 50 items maximum (2) Terminated immediately upon active browser shutdown context (3) 4096 Bytes. Select the correct code:

trick: Trap: Forgetting to declare an expiration date on a cookie. It reverts to a session cookie and disappears the moment the user closes the app window, causing data loss!
tip: Cookies use tiny storage limits and rely on explicit dates to persist data.

question: Consider the following statements regarding browser hard reload shortcuts: Statement 1: Pressing 'Ctrl + F5' or 'Ctrl + Shift + R' in modern web browsers forces a hard reload, completely bypassing the local cache directory to fetch fresh files from the server. Statement 2: Hard reloading can override and update malicious core registry blocks embedded inside the host computer's motherboard BIOS firmware chip. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Hard reload signals the app to clear out current view parameters and download fresh elements. Step 2: Browser shortcut actions are limited strictly to high-level application data layers; they cannot reach or manipulate underlying motherboard BIOS firmware chips. Statement 2 is false.
trick: Trap: Clicking 'Refresh' over and over to see a website change. Standard reload reads old cache! Use 'Ctrl + F5' to force a deep download from the root server.
tip: Ctrl + F5 clears local browser memory caches to pull updated web data.

question: Match List I with List II regarding international URL extensions: List I: (A) Generic Top-Level Domain (gTLD) (B) Country Code Top-Level Domain (ccTLD) (C) Sponsored Top-Level Domain (sTLD). List II: (1) .in / .uk (2) .gov / .mil (3) .com / .net. Select the correct code:

question: Consider the following statements regarding Cookie hijacking: Statement 1: If a hacker intercepts your unencrypted session cookie via public Wi-Fi, they can paste it into their own browser and log into your account without knowing your password. Statement 2: Setting the 'HttpOnly' flag inside your browser settings prevents hackers from copying physical files off your local computer hard drive. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: This is a Session Hijacking (or cookie side-jacking) attack. The server validates the cookie string, not the person, so possessing the key gives profile access. Step 2: 'HttpOnly' stops malicious JavaScript from stealing cookies from the browser memory; it cannot protect physical hard drive files from being copied. Statement 2 is false.
trick: Trap: Logging into financial services on public Wi-Fi without HTTPS. Hackers pick up your raw session cookies right out of the air waves to clone your session!
tip: Session cookies act as digital entry keys. Secure them with HTTPS and HttpOnly configurations.

question: Match List I with List II regarding Search Engine visibility commands: List I: (A) Noindex tag (B) Nofollow tag (C) Disallow directive. List II: (1) Instructs spiders not to track or pass authority to specific hyperlinks on a webpage (2) A string in robots.txt blocking crawlers from entering a specific directory folder (3) An HTML meta tag instructing search engines completely avoid listing that page in search results. Select the correct code:
explanation: Step 1: Meta 'noindex' blocks pages from popping up in public search results. Step 2: 'nofollow' cuts crawler links evaluation tracks. Step 3: 'Disallow' parameters block bots right at the robots.txt directory gateway layer.

tip: Disallow keeps bots out of folders. Noindex keeps pages out of public searches entirely.

question: Consider the following statements regarding the behavior of URL tracking fragments: Statement 1: UTM (Urchin Tracking Module) parameters are appended to URLs using query strings (like '?utm_source=bank') to track marketing campaign traffic metrics. Statement 2: Adding a UTM tracking suffix completely changes the target website layout architecture, forcing the server to build a unique webpage database file. tip: UTM queries track marketing referral data without altering the layout architecture of the webpage.

question: Match List I with List II regarding web infrastructure terms: List I: (A) URL (B) URN (C) URI. List II: (1) Uniform Resource Name (identifies a resource uniquely by name regardless of its location, like an ISBN book code) (2) Uniform Resource Identifier (the overarching overarching parent classification standard) (3) Uniform Resource Locator (specifies the location and access method of an online resource). tip: URI is the parent standard. URL locates web files. URN names resources persistently.

question: Consider the following statements regarding tracking cookies data lifetimes: Statement 1: Setting a cookie's expiration date to a historical past date forces the browser client application to delete it from disk immediately. Statement 2: Browser cookies can store and execute micro-assembly loops to automatically accelerate local hard drive file index formatting scripts. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Forcing a timestamp backward tricks the browser's cleanup loop into purging the expired data record instantly. Step 2: Cookies are basic, flat text strings; they possess absolutely zero processing logic or code execution capacity. Statement 2 is false.

tip: Setting expiration parameters to past dates commands browsers to delete cookies immediately.

question: Match List I with List II regarding email payload alternatives: List I: (A) File exceeds 25 MB cap (B) Bulk messaging delivery framework (C) Raw text representation schema. List II: (1) Google Drive Link (2) MIME format (3) Mail Merge / SMTP server pipe clusters. Select the correct code:
explanation: Step 1: Size overflow forces data routing outside raw email parameters to Drive storage modules. Step 2: Enterprise campaigns rely on dedicated SMTP pipeline arrays to bypass bulk rate limits. Step 3: MIME formats allow binary images to travel disguised as alphanumeric text strings inside standard mail packets.
trick: Trap: Attaching 10 high-res photos to one mail. The email app will reject it for layout overflow limits! Share a cloud drive folder address link to bypass the size cap.
tip: Drive integration bypasses the 25 MB email attachment bottleneck smoothly.

question: Consider the following statements regarding the Indexing behavior of duplicated content: Statement 1: Search engine optimization uses a 'Canonical Tag' (rel='canonical') to identify the master version of a webpage when duplicate copies exist across different URLs. Statement 2: If multiple identical pages exist without a canonical tag, Googlebot will double your site traffic metrics by indexing all copies separately. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Canonical tags act as traffic signposts, steering crawlers to prioritize one official source link asset. Step 2: Spiders penalize duplicate content blocks; they flag duplicate arrays as spam and downrank the entire domain. Statement 2 is false.
trick: Trap: Having 'website.com' and 'website.com/index.html' look exactly the same. Spiders see these as separate pages and might rank you lower for duplicate content! Use canonical tags to fix it.
tip: Canonical tags clarify master site links to avoid duplicate content optimization penalties.

question: Match List I with List II regarding browser local storage boundaries: List I: (A) SessionStorage (B) LocalStorage (C) Standard Cookies. List II: (1) Stores persistent data up to 5-10 MB that never expires unless cleared manually via code (2) Stores data up to 5 MB that is completely cleared the millisecond the specific browser tab closes (3) Stores tiny 4 KB data segments that are continuously transmitted to the server with every HTTP request header. Select the correct code:
explanation: Step 1: SessionStorage locks limits per active window instance context. Step 2: LocalStorage provides massive offline database slots inside the user browser layout without expiring. Step 3: Cookies are small but travel across every internet query hop, eating up precious network upload speed if bloated.
trick: Trap: Putting large user data in cookies. Every time you open a link, those cookies are zipped up and uploaded to the server, slowing down your network speed! Use LocalStorage for big files.
tip: Cookies travel with every server request. LocalStorage saves massive files completely offline.

question: Consider the following statements regarding URL subdirectories vs query handling: Statement 1: A URL directory structure path like '/products/books/' is processed as a hierarchical folder layout design by web servers. Statement 2: A query parameter link like '?category=books' passes processing variables directly to a backend script engine or database index filter. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Subdirectory structures navigate structural node layout hierarchies. Step 2: Query parameters feed processing variables directly to code scripts to run data operations on databases dynamically. Both statements align with internet routing logic.
trick: Trap: Thinking paths are always real folders on a hard drive. Modern websites use clean routing code to make dynamic script queries (?id=1) look like pretty folder structures (/products/1/) to rank better on Google!
tip: Paths navigate folder nodes, queries deliver dynamic database search parameters.

question: Match List I with List II regarding search index freshness constraints: List I: (A) Sitemaps (B) Crawl Frequency (C) Cache Snapshot. List II: (1) The historic text backup copy of a page saved in the search engine's directory data grid (2) XML directory maps submitted by webmasters to guide crawlers to internal site links (3) Dictates how often a bot returns to scan a site, varying based on domain authority updates. Select the correct code:
explanation: Step 1: XML Sitemaps act as navigation roadmaps for indexing spiders. Step 2: Crawl frequency shifts based on how often a site posts updates (news sites get crawled every minute, personal blogs once a month). Step 3: Cache snapshots show your site's history.
trick: Trap: Submitting an XML sitemap does not guarantee immediate Google indexing! It only suggests paths; Googlebot schedules the actual visit based on your site's authority metrics.
tip: Sitemaps list paths, frequency tracks tracking cadence, snapshots preserve search database history archives.

question: Consider the following statements regarding the safety bounds of cookie deletion tools: Statement 1: Anti-malware software frequently flags and isolates tracking cookies because cookies can mutate into active virus code blocks over time. Statement 2: Tracking cookies are deleted purely because they compromise user privacy by monitoring commercial footprints across cross-site domains. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Cookies lack any structural executable formatting; they cannot hold or transform into logic engines or virus strains. Statement 1 is false. Step 2: Their cleanup focuses on protecting personal behavior privacy bounds from profiling aggregations. Therefore, Statement 2 is true.
trick: Trap: Fearing a 'Tracking Cookie' warning like it's a virus. It can't break your computer or steal files! It just reports your shopping habits to ad networks.
tip: Cookies are inert configuration text data matrices; they affect privacy profile layouts, never hardware integrity.

question: Match List I with List II regarding secure link protocol handling: List I: (A) HTTP Port 80 (B) HTTPS Port 443 (C) HSTS Header. List II: (1) Commands the browser to forcefully convert all unencrypted connection attempts to HTTPS locally before sending traffic (2) Operates data in clear text structures open to packet sniffer tracking (3) Wraps URL data blocks in encrypted TLS session handshakes. Select the correct code:
explanation: Step 1: Port 80 runs insecure clear-text text lines. Step 2: Port 443 processes secure encrypted website data streams. Step 3: HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) forces local browser clients to auto-upgrade unencrypted requests instantly to stop data leaks.
trick: Trap: Typing 'http://' to test a site but seeing it auto-switch to 'https://'. That is the powerful HSTS security header forcing your browser to protect your session before a single bit leaves your PC!
tip: HSTS blocks unencrypted protocol downgrades entirely within the browser software client engine layers.

question: Consider the following statements regarding the architectural function of domain names: Statement 1: Domain names are case-sensitive; typing 'www.SSC.nic.in' will fail to connect if the server profile registration is locked in lowercase format. Statement 2: The domain name structure acts as a user-friendly alias system to mask complex numerical computer network destination coordinates. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Global DNS routing standards enforce strict case-insensitivity on host domain names; capitalization variants route to identical IP destinations flawlessly. Statement 1 is false. Step 2: Alphanumeric addresses provide memorable aliases for human navigation over binary network arrays. Statement 2 is true.
trick: Trap: Capitalizing domain paths. While the domain name part is case-insensitive (sSc.In works), the file folder path trailing it (/ExAm/test.html) can be strictly case-sensitive depending on the server OS architecture!
tip: Domain names are case-insensitive aliases mapping to static or dynamic IP targets.

question: Match List I with List II regarding browser cookie lifespans: List I: (A) Session Cookie duration (B) Max-Age attribute parameter (C) Cookie with a date set to 01-Jan-1970. List II: (1) Defines durability persistence limits in exact seconds from the active connection time (2) Instantly commands the system database to wipe the cookie file records from local disk storage blocks (3) Bound to the lifespan of the parent runtime execution window layer. Select the correct code:
explanation: Step 1: Session tracking lives and dies with browser processes. Step 2: Max-Age sets clean duration limits in counting seconds (e.g., 3600 for one hour). Step 3: Historic timestamps trick data management tools into firing instant storage block file purges.
trick: Trap: Setting cookie life to a year away. If a user clears their browser settings data manually, all persistent cookies are wiped instantly regardless of your future expiration date timestamps!
tip: Max-Age handles cookie life math in precise seconds; past dates cause instant deletion.

question: Consider the following statements regarding the architectural limits of a Web Crawler traversal pattern: Statement 1: Crawlers trace links recursively, prioritizing deep nested directories before scanning the home root index nodes on a fresh domain. Statement 2: Spiders use explicit crawling algorithms like Breadth-First Search (BFS) to map broad structural top-level domain surfaces systematically. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Spiders prioritize high-level, structural surface paths first before diving into deep subfolder trees. Statement 1 is false. Step 2: BFS algorithms allow search bots to index the most important high-level landing templates across the internet efficiently. Statement 2 is correct.
trick: Trap: Thinking spiders wander randomly. They use highly structured mathematical graph traversal rules (like BFS) to optimize their limited time on a server link landscape!
tip: Crawlers prioritize wide surface mapping patterns over crawling deep silo subdirectories first.

question: Match List I with List II regarding specific URL encoding conversions: List I: (A) Space character (B) Question mark character (C) Ampersand character. List II: (1) %26 (2) %20 (3) %3F. Select the correct code:
explanation: Step 1: Spaces translate to character array '%20'. Step 2: The structural query initiator '?' converts to ASCII percentage value '%3F'. Step 3: Parameter separator '&' shifts to hexadecimal encoding index code '%26'.
trick: Trap: Typing data values containing real '&' or '?' characters into form query fields. The browser must convert them to hex code equivalents (%26) so they don't break the URL syntax parsing engine rules!
tip: URL encoding translates structural reservation symbols into plain hex strings to preserve database transfer arguments.

question: Consider the following statements regarding the structural limits of browser local asset Cache: Statement 1: Browsers can completely cache and freeze dynamic SQL database queries locally, displaying live real-time financial market numbers without querying the remote data center server. Statement 2: Cache parameters are optimized strictly for static, unchanging file payloads like website stylesheet configurations, script frameworks, and product logos. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Cache systems cannot store live server-side database streams locally; financial numbers require continuous remote API calls to ensure accuracy. Statement 1 is false. Step 2: Local cache architecture is explicitly designed to keep heavy static files (images, CSS) on hand to minimize redundant web transfers. Statement 2 is correct.
trick: Trap: Caching dynamic bank account pages. This would be a massive security disaster! Browsers strictly configure live transaction pages to bypass cache storage blocks entirely.
tip: Cache rules apply strictly to static layout assets, never to live server database queries.

question: Match List I with List II regarding search index extraction barriers: List I: (A) Captcha forms (B) Orphan Page (C) No-image index rule. List II: (1) A webpage that has zero inbound structural links pointing to it, making it impossible for a Crawler to discover naturally (2) Artificial intelligence gates explicitly engineered to block indexing bots from scraping data (3) Directs search engines to parse text files but omit image binaries from media search index files. Select the correct code:
explanation: Step 1: Captchas are defensive filters stopping automated bots. Step 2: Spiders can only discover pages by following existing web paths; a page with zero incoming links is an isolated 'Orphan' page. Step 3: Media rules filter out graphical payloads from textual indexing directories.
trick: Trap: Creating a new page but forgetting to link to it anywhere on your site map. It becomes a ghost 'Orphan' page that Googlebot can never find or list automatically!
tip: Orphan pages escape crawler tracking. Captchas act as wall blocks filtering automated tracking scripts.

question: Consider the following statements regarding the 'Port' section within a standard URL string: Statement 1: If a user omits the port number in a standard URL string (e.g., typing 'https://example.com'), the browser automatically defaults to target Port 80 for HTTPS traffic. Statement 2: The default port assignment for standard, unencrypted HTTP traffic is Port 80, while secure encrypted HTTPS traffic points natively to Port 443. Which of the statements is/are correct?
explanation: Step 1: Omitting the port on an 'https://' scheme directs the browser client to target secure Port 443 automatically, not Port 80. Statement 1 is false. Step 2: Global IANA networking standards map standard clear-text web traffic to Port 80 and secure web data tunnels to Port 443. Statement 2 is correct.
trick: Trap: Browsers hide port numbers to keep links pretty. Typing 'https://example.com' invisibly appends ':443' to the end of the address string to route your network packets correctly!
tip: HTTP traffic defaults to Port 80. Secure HTTPS automatically targets Port 443.
